The FD-TD method was first proposed by Yee in 1966 but gained serious attention in the late 1970s and 1980s.
FD-TD uses central differences in time and space on an orthogonal grid with an explicit leap-frog time integration scheme.
FD-TD can model electromagnetic structures as large as 5,000 cubic wavelengths.
Finite element-like methods use interpolation functions with continuous first derivatives inside elements to approximate fields.
Point-matched finite element methods use dual complementary meshes for electric and magnetic fields.
Gauss' law is enforced with second-order accuracy in FD-TD on orthogonal grids but violated on non-orthogonal grids.
Numerical dispersion causes the numerical phase velocity to depend on wavelength, grid size, and propagation direction.
Higher-order FD-TD schemes using fourth-order spatial derivatives reduce phase errors significantly.
The stability condition for FD-TD time step on a cubic lattice is Δt ≤ h / (u_max * sqrt(3)).
Non-uniform grids cause numerical reflections at interfaces due to changes in numerical phase velocity.
Modified finite volume methods cast Maxwell's equations in conservation form and allow general polyhedral grids.
Spurious non-physical modes may appear in finite element time-domain simulations due to Gauss' law violation.
Boundary conditions on perfect conductors enforce zero tangential electric field components.
The leap-frog scheme staggers electric and magnetic fields in time for second-order accuracy.
Numerical reflection coefficient depends on grid cell sizes and numerical phase velocities on each side of the interface.
Stair-stepped approximations in FD-TD limit geometry representation accuracy for curved boundaries.
Explicit time integration schemes avoid solving simultaneous equations, improving computational efficiency.
The point-matched method requires finite element interpolation functions with continuous first derivatives.
Proper mesh generation is critical to maintain orthogonality and minimize spurious modes and numerical errors.
Numerical dispersion errors become significant for wavelengths less than about 10 times the grid cell size.
